summary: Specifies Verifiable Random Functions, a public-key version of a keyed hash. Only the secret key holder can compute the output, but anyone with the public key can check it. It gives RSA and elliptic-curve constructions. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Only you can roll a special dice, but anyone can check that the roll was honest and could not have been picked on purpose.

questions: what is a verifiable random function
subtitle: The public-key version of a keyed hash function with proof of correctness.

tldr.problem: Hash-based data structures are vulnerable to enumeration attacks: an attacker can guess every item in a hash table by computing all possible hashes offline.
tldr.mechanism: A VRF is like a keyed hash that produces both a hash output and a proof. Only the secret key holder can compute hashes, but anyone with the public key can verify the proof and confirm the hash is correct.
tldr.outcome: Attackers cannot enumerate the data structure without querying the key holder, and the verifier can check that queries are answered honestly.

facts.label: Core security property
facts.value: Uniqueness: one output per input per key

today: RFC 9381 is an Informational RFC that represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group. It defines the VRF constructions and their security properties, with implementations available in cryptographic libraries and active use in blockchain and consensus systems.

sections.title: What is a Verifiable Random Function?
sections.content:
A Verifiable Random Function (VRF) is the public-key version of a keyed cryptographic hash. It lets only the holder of the secret key compute a hash output, but anyone with the public key can verify that the output is correct.

A VRF comes with three algorithms. The Prover (holder of the secret key) uses VRF_prove(SK, alpha) to compute a proof that they have correctly hashed an input. The VRF_hash(SK, alpha) function computes the hash output directly. The Verifier (holder only of the public key) uses VRF_verify(PK, alpha, pi) to check the proof and extract the hash output.

The key property is uniqueness: for any input alpha and any honest public key, there is exactly one valid hash output beta. This prevents the Prover from producing two different hashes for the same input, even if they try to cheat.
sections.plainLanguage: A VRF is a special function where you keep one key secret and one key public. With your secret key, you can compute a random-looking number from any input and prove it is correct. Anyone with your public key can check that your number really was computed honestly.

sections.title: Key Security Properties
sections.content:
VRFs are designed to provide several security properties. Full uniqueness means an adversary cannot find two different outputs for the same input, even with a maliciously generated public key. Full collision resistance means an adversary cannot find two different inputs with the same output, again even with malicious keys.

Full pseudorandomness ensures that the hash output is indistinguishable from a random value to anyone who does not know the secret key, even if they know multiple other inputs and outputs. Unpredictability under malicious key generation is a property where if the input has enough entropy, the output is unpredictable no matter how the keys were generated. This property is important for some consensus protocols.

The RFC defines two variants of these properties: trusted versions that only hold if keys are generated correctly, and full versions that hold even against malicious key generation.
sections.plainLanguage: VRFs are secure in several ways. Nobody can find two different answers for the same question. The answers look like random noise to someone who does not know the secret key. And if you feed in something with real randomness, the output is unpredictable even if someone tries to trick the system.

sections.title: RSA Full Domain Hash VRF
sections.content:
The RSA-FDH-VRF (Fully Domain Hash) uses RSA cryptography. The Prover computes a proof by signing the input with the RSA private key using the Full Domain Hash algorithm. The hash output is computed by hashing the proof with a cryptographic hash function (SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512). Verification simply verifies the RSA signature and hashes the result.

The security of RSA-FDH-VRF follows from the standard RSA assumption: the difficulty of factoring the RSA modulus. It provides trusted uniqueness, trusted collision resistance, and full pseudorandomness. However, it does not provide full uniqueness or unpredictability under malicious key generation, so it is vulnerable to weak or maliciously-chosen keys.

The RFC defines three ciphersuites: RSA-FDH-VRF-SHA256, RSA-FDH-VRF-SHA384, and RSA-FDH-VRF-SHA512, parameterized by the RSA key size and hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: The RSA version uses RSA signatures. You sign the input with your secret key, then hash the signature to get the final answer. Anyone can check the signature with your public key.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve VRF
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve VRF (ECVRF) uses elliptic curve cryptography instead of RSA. The Prover picks a random nonce k and computes Gamma = x*H (where x is the secret scalar and H is a point on the curve derived from the input) and other values, then computes a challenge c via a hash, and finally s = k + c*x mod q. The proof is the point Gamma concatenated with the values c and s.

The hash output is derived from Gamma via a hash function applied to it with domain separation. Verification recomputes the challenge from public values and checks that it matches the one in the proof.

ECVRF with proper key validation provides full uniqueness, trusted collision resistance, full pseudorandomness, and crucially, unpredictability under malicious key generation. This stronger property makes ECVRF suitable for leader selection in consensus protocols. The RFC provides ciphersuites for NIST curves (P-256, P-384, P-521) and Edwards curves (edwards25519, edwards448).
sections.plainLanguage: The elliptic curve version uses points on a mathematical curve. The Prover computes a point on the curve from the input, creates a proof using curve arithmetic, and anyone can verify the proof using just the public key.

sections.title: Common Uses
sections.content:
The main application of VRFs is defending against enumeration attacks on hash-based data structures. When a Prover holds a VRF secret key and builds a data structure on top of VRF hashes, only the Prover can answer queries about whether data is in the structure. Yet anyone with the public key can verify the answers are correct, preventing the Prover from giving false answers.

VRFs are also useful in leader selection for consensus protocols, where unpredictability prevents adversaries from predicting who will be leader ahead of time. They appear in blockchains and other distributed systems. Other uses include Verifiable Shuffle, Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRFs), and certificate transparency mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: VRFs are used to keep secrets hidden in shared data structures (only the key holder can look up entries, but anyone can verify the answers) and to make random choices in blockchains fairly (you cannot predict who will lead until after the randomness is revealed).

sections.title: Security and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Proper key generation is critical: keys MUST be generated using the specified key generation algorithm, not chosen adversarially. The VRF output beta is always distinguishable from random by anyone who knows the secret key or a valid proof for that input, even if the output alone looks random.

Side-channel attacks are a concern: implementations MUST use constant-time arithmetic for elliptic curves and other operations to prevent timing leaks. Do not use rejection sampling (try-and-increment) methods; they have been shown to leak timing information about secrets.

The VRF output alone does not provide secrecy for the input: if you know the output and suspect a few possible inputs, you can check them via the proof verification. And if input hashes are prehashed (to use a VRF with a hash function different from its native one), care must be taken to use proper domain separation to prevent ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations need to use proper random number generation, do arithmetic in constant time to avoid timing leaks, and ensure the input is not revealed by the output.

viz.caption: RSA-FDH and ECVRF provide different trade-offs in security properties.

left.title: RSA-FDH-VRF
left.desc: Trusted uniqueness, trusted collision resistance, full pseudorandomness. Does not prevent malicious key generation attacks.

right.title: ECVRF
right.desc: Full uniqueness, full pseudorandomness, and unpredictability under malicious keys (with validation). Better for consensus protocols.
